_comment: All the copy for /work/making-the-app-testable, in reading order. Editable in the browser under `npm run dev`, or in bulk via `npm run copy:export`. Drafted 2026-08-06 from rohitsehmi.com/apps — everything not marked [NEEDS:] is on that page or follows directly from it. It draws on three initiatives that page keeps separate (A Contextual Home, Search Experience, Small Enhancements) because they are one argument: two structural rebuilds that made testing possible, and the programme that ran through them. Kept deliberately short — a reader asks for a complex flow made simple, not for length.
title: The app that could not be tested
standfirst: Hotels.com's two most valuable screens were both fixed layouts. Nothing on them could vary, so nothing could be learned from them. Rebuilding both as systems is what turned the app into something the team could run a continuous testing programme through.

contribution.detail: Senior Product Designer — UX, mobile and brand
[NEEDS: the decisions, not the deliverables. This study carries the strongest numbers in the portfolio, so it is the first thing a reviewer will want.]
Product, design, engineering and analytics, running a continuous multivariate testing programme

problem.heading: The problem
problem.standfirst: A layout that cannot vary cannot be tested, and these were the two screens where testing mattered most.
paras: Hotels.com sells in 90 points of sale and 41 languages, lists properties in over 200 countries, and takes around 165,000 bookings a day. Every one of those customers met the same two screens: a dated, static home, and a search results page built on a fixed card framework.

Both were arrangements rather than systems. Nothing on either could respond to who was looking or what they were in the middle of — and because nothing could vary, no question about what a traveller actually needed to see could be answered. The app shipped on judgement and defended it afterwards.

[NEEDS: the insight. What did you know about how people were failing on these screens? One research finding turns this from a refactor into a decision, and a reader scores it as the first thing it looks for.]

process.heading: How it was worked out
process.standfirst: Rebuild both screens as systems, then run everything through one programme rather than shipping one-off launches.
process.openingPara: The home moved from a fixed layout to a modular, scalable one, with a single brand language holding it together across iOS and Android — the first personalisation work the company had done. Search results moved from static cards to dynamic ones, so a card could carry different amounts of content in the same slot. Neither was a visual exercise. Both were about making the screen capable of holding a variation.

principle._note: One paragraph, three editable parts, because the middle is emphasised. Editing is plain text, so a <strong> inside a single string would be stripped the first time anyone touched it.
principle.before: What ran through them was a standing programme across product, design, engineering and analytics, built to fail fast and iterate. Its operating principle, in the words used at the time:
principle.quote: create a hypothesis to give us an opportunity to learn, not to predict.
principle.after: That distinction is what makes a losing test useful rather than embarrassing, and it is why the one below was kept rather than quietly dropped.

process.closingPara: The 2019 refresh pushed the same idea further: a global rebrand with parity across platforms, machine learning behind modules like recommended destinations and travel guides, and a shift towards content before, during and after a trip rather than only at the point of booking.
process.explorationsHeading: Three tests, and what each one settled

explorations.title: A richer image gallery, on Android
explorations.why: Won. Positive on conversion, more interaction with the gallery, and it sent better-qualified shoppers through to the booking form. The variation was only possible because the card had become a container rather than a fixed arrangement.
explorations.imageAlt: The Android image gallery variant tested on the search results card

explorations.title: A search recap carrying check-in details, on iOS
explorations.why: Lost. Negative on conversion, so it went back out and was retested without the check-in details. Showing travellers a summary of what they had already told us cost more attention than it returned.
explorations.imageAlt: The search recap variant that carried check-in details

interface.heading: The two screens
interface.standfirst: A home whose modules changed with context, and a results card that could hold a different amount of content in the same slot.

impact.heading: Impact
impact.standfirst: The home's numbers are the hard ones. The framework underneath both screens is what everything after them was tested inside.
impact.metricsSource: [NEEDS: these four are the contextual home result, recorded as an overall strong positive. paras: +85% on account creation beside +5% on conversion is the finding worth stating: a contextual screen was far better at starting a relationship than at closing a booking. Sign-ins and engagement moved with account creation and point the same way.
